GeoGPT geology workshop · Keep this lesson open

Has the sand ended, or is its image blurred?

A borehole samples one place underground. To follow a sand layer between boreholes, geologists also use returning sound-like seismic pulses. Reflections from a thin layer can overlap. You will ask GeoGPT to calculate two images of exactly the same sand bed and see why a blurred image need not mean the sand has disappeared.

What you will learn

Separate a change in the rocks from a change in how the rocks are imaged.

The computer task: one supplied model file and one prompt.

The lesson supplies every setting. You do not have to invent a question, read a paper or write code.

Four words, explained here

Borehole
A drilled hole that provides observations at one location.

Reflection
Part of a seismic pulse that returns from a boundary between rocks.

Wedge
A layer that is thin at one end and thick at the other.

Pulse length
How long one returning signal lasts. A shorter pulse can separate nearby boundaries more clearly in this model.

Next: Understand the result ↓

Understand the result, one point at a time

The supplied text file contains a ready-to-run model with the rock speeds, densities, layer shape and pulse settings. GeoGPT executes it and checks that no signal is produced when the layer vanishes or when both rocks have identical acoustic properties. You do not need to choose a wavelet, write an equation or answer a hypothesis question.

Start with the top picture: the rocks.

Yellow is the sand layer. It is thin at the left and thick at the right. This is a made-up geological model with known geometry, not a field discovery.

Compare the two lower pictures: the signals.

They show the same rocks with a longer and a shorter pulse. Red and blue mean opposite signal directions, not different rock types. The vertical axis is travel time down and back, not depth.

Look near the thin end.

Ask whether two separate boundaries are as easy to see in both signal images. The dashed lines mark the true model boundaries; they are not features independently discovered by the AI.

A tempting claim to check

“The seismic image is faint, so the aquifer must end.” An imaging effect is another possible explanation. This model does not establish whether real sand contains water or whether water can flow through it.

Talk it through

Use your own result. Speak to a partner or think quietly; you do not have to type an answer.

  1. Point to one thing held fixed between the two signal pictures.
  2. Point to one thing that changed. Is that change in the sand or in its image?
  3. What could a borehole observation tell you that these synthetic images cannot?
After discussing: read an example explanation

The rock layer is identical in both simulations. Changing the pulse changes how clearly its boundaries can be separated. A merged reflection therefore does not, by itself, prove that the sand ends. Actual borehole observations are needed before interpreting real ground.

Optional: try one idea

The required investigation is already complete. If you have time, use this suggestion or explain an idea of your own before trying it.

Ask GeoGPT: “Preserve the original results. Recalculate the same sand bed at 30 Hz only. Save a separate image called sand-bed-extra.png using the same axes and colors. Explain one difference in ordinary language. Do not change rock properties or ask for settings.”

Optional research background and sources

Modern seismic interpretation uses simulations to test competing explanations. This exercise teaches the basic controlled comparison behind that work. It is foundational, not a new seismic method, and does not reproduce a full recent-paper workflow.
